zq.types: ZQ is a set of wool sourcing standards, now run by Zentera, the company formerly called The New Zealand Merino Company, which has worked with growers under the ZQ name since 2007. The base ZQ standard is a third-party audited farm standard covering animal welfare, environmental integrity and social responsibility; it prohibits mulesing. ZQ+, formerly called ZQRX (the ZQ Regenerative Index), builds on ZQ with a regenerative agriculture program that measures and improves farm outcomes over time. Zentera also supplies wool certified to Textile Exchange's Responsible Wool Standard. None of these grades the fiber itself: micron, staple length and strength are specified separately, and ZQ is best known for fine merino.
zq.fabrics: ZQ merino goes into the same products as other fine wool: base layers, T-shirts, socks, knitwear, activewear, outdoor midlayers and suiting. Outdoor and performance apparel brands have been prominent users; Helly Hansen, for example, has described bringing ZQRX (now ZQ+) wool into base layers. Because the standard concerns farms and supply, the fabrics are ordinary wool constructions: worsted jersey, interlock and rib knits, woollen-spun sweaters and worsted suiting, sometimes blended with nylon or elastane.
zq.quality: The ZQ or ZQ+ mark on a hangtag indicates the wool came from audited growers, but it says nothing about fineness, so read the label for wool percentage and, if given, micron. For merino next to skin, fibers finer than about 20 microns generally feel soft, while coarser wool can prickle. Ask the brand whether the whole wool content is ZQ or only part of it, and check whether blends include nylon or elastane. Genuine program participation can be confirmed with the brand or Zentera. Quality signs are the usual ones for wool: dense, even knitting, clean seams, low pilling on a rub test, and shrink-resist information for machine-washable items.
pros: The base standard prohibits mulesing, according to the program.
Farms are audited by a third party against published animal welfare, environmental and social requirements.
The ZQ+ regenerative program adds measured farm-level outcomes beyond a pass or fail audit.
Traceability links wool to participating growers, mainly in New Zealand.
cons: The mark does not specify fiber quality, so ZQ wool can still be coarse or prickly if the grade is wrong.
Program standards are set by the commercial company that sells the wool, not by an independent standards body.
Regenerative outcomes are program-defined metrics whose independent verification is still developing.
Certified wool usually costs more than conventional wool.
zq.impact: Wool's footprint is dominated by the farm: land use, enteric methane from sheep, fertilizer and pasture management, with scouring water and energy downstream. ZQ addresses farm practices through audited standards and ZQ+ through regenerative metrics, but no independent comparison of ZQ farms against conventional farms was found for this entry, so claimed benefits are program statements. Animal welfare is where the standard is most specific: it bans mulesing, the removal of skin strips from the breech to prevent flystrike. Peer-reviewed Australian research supports the idea that alternatives to surgical mulesing reduce harm; a 2012 study in the Australian Veterinary Journal (Hemsworth and colleagues) found behavioral effects on lambs of plastic breech clips were smaller than those of surgical mulesing. Flystrike control without mulesing still needs breeding and management.
zq.care: ZQ does not change care; follow merino guidance and the label. Machine-washable merino (shrink-resist treated) can go on a wool or gentle cycle at 30 C or cooler, inside out, with a wool detergent free of protease enzymes and bleach. Untreated wool should be hand washed in lukewarm water with minimal agitation, since heat plus friction causes felting. Dry flat in the shade, reshaping while damp; do not tumble dry unless permitted. Steam or iron on the wool setting with a press cloth. De-pill with a comb. Store clean and dry with cedar or in sealed bags, as moth and carpet-beetle larvae eat keratin.
faq: What does ZQ mean on a wool label?

It means the wool came from growers audited under the ZQ standard, run by Zentera (formerly The New Zealand Merino Company), covering animal welfare, environment and social responsibility. It does not describe the wool's fineness or quality.

Yes, according to the program, which states that mulesing is not permitted on properties supplying ZQ wool. Growers manage flystrike through other strategies. This is a program claim verified through its farm audits.
What is the difference between ZQ and ZQ+?

ZQ is the base audited farm standard. ZQ+, formerly called ZQRX, is a regenerative program that builds on it by measuring and working to improve farm outcomes such as soil and biodiversity over time. Both are run by Zentera.
Is ZQ the same as the Responsible Wool Standard?

No. The Responsible Wool Standard is a Textile Exchange standard; ZQ is a company-run program. Both prohibit mulesing, but they differ in governance and detail. Zentera also supplies RWS-certified wool alongside ZQ.
notable: The company behind ZQ renamed itself Zentera, and its regenerative program ZQRX was renamed ZQ+.
The program describes ZQ as the first accredited wool fiber to guarantee that mulesing does not occur, a claim based on its farm audits.
